title: I tried five ways to improve my Claude Code plugin. None passed my own bar.
summary:
I built Off the Wall, a plugin for Claude Code and Codex. It saves the corrections you give your agent and shows them again, word for word, when you ask for something similar later. This post is about what did not work, because that is where I learned the most.

What I can say it does

A model can't know how you write commit messages or dates. I made up 11 habits like that and turned them into tasks, 3 runs each, 33 runs per condition, run headless.

  • Claude Sonnet without the plugin followed the habit 2 times out of 33. With it: 20.
  • With haiku: 1 to 17 in the first run, and 2 to 25 in a rerun.

These are habits I invented, not real users' records. I fixed a grader bug after seeing results, so the rerun is not an independent replication. I have not measured Opus or the Codex models.

The problem I tried to fix

The plugin also attaches quotes to unrelated requests. On 8 prompts that have nothing to do with the stored corrections, it attached 1.8 quotes on average. I had written "if nothing is similar, nothing is attached". That was false, and I corrected it publicly.

So I tried to cut that noise without losing the useful quotes. I wrote the plan and the pass bar first, then ran each idea.

Five attempts

  1. Word conditions (two shared words, or one rare word). On 150 stored corrections, unrelated quotes dropped from 6.0 to 2.0. On 240 corrections with repeated habits it went from 6.0 to 5.5. It did not generalize. Dropped.
  2. Six variants for short inputs. None passed the bar. Kept the existing guard.
  3. A small local embedding model (all-MiniLM-L6-v2). One setting cut noise a lot but lost too many useful quotes on held-out cases. Three more settings failed the same bar. Dropped.
  4. Show the original request next to each correction. Quote only: 20 of 33. Quote plus request: 19 of 33. No gain. Not added.
  5. Merge repeats of the same correction (an idea from a wiki-style memory). 18/40 against 20/40, a gain of 11%. My bar was 25%. Rejected.

What I learned besides the results

  • The runner cut my selection at 3 quotes in two experiments. The default is 6. I found it, wrote it down and left the original numbers in.
  • One task's grader was wrong and I re-scored it after the fact. The original table stays, with the correction next to it.
  • Passing my own tests never meant it helps real users. The real test is whether your own corrections pile up and come back at the right time. I do not have that evidence yet.

Code, plans, data and every failed run: https://github.com/toranalytics/off-the-wall (docs/). A plain-language overview: https://toranalytics.github.io/en/otw-what-it-does/

If an unrelated quote shows up in your session, or a needed one is missing, an issue would help a lot. You do not need to send your original text.

title: Blazar Video Encoder for Generative Video
summary:
Lately I've been using video diffusion models and learning more about them. As I was digging around the various codebases I noticed that there were a couple of common approaches to actually encoding the frames that are generated by the diffusion models: mainly use PyAV or shell out to FFmpeg. There's nothing especially wrong with either of these approaches but I think it is possible for us to do a little better. So I (along with my robot friends) built Blazar. You can find the code repo for Blazar here.

Today with PyAV the flow is roughly:

  1. Convert tensor from BF16 or F32 to u8 and reshape to (H, W, C)
  2. D2H transfer
  3. RGB to YUV conversion
  4. (if NVENC) upload to the GPU
  5. Encode

So, I think, this is roughly what we want to do:

  1. Be able to take the native output tensor shape of the model as an input. (B, C, T, H, W) seems to be the common tensor shape but a video encoder will want more like (B, T, H, W, C) or (B, T, C, H, W) (or whatever nv12 is with U' and V' interleaved)
  2. Do a fused YUV + tensor reshape conversion (does that count as a reshape? maybe not) either on GPU or CPU
  3. Encode either using NVENC (or some other HW encoder) or a variety of software encoders
  4. Be relatively easily configurable...
  5. Probably don't get in the way of the Python GIL

So the robot and I landed on a design where most of the work happens in Rust. Backends for YUV conversion and encoding are swappable between hardware and software so that if you would prefer not to use HW for YUV conversion and encoding you don't have to do that. There is a concept of "Calibrations" that are keyed on model and target quality so you can have multiple calibrations with different latency or quality targets and make them configurable by model. These live in human readable TOML files.

import blazar

cals = blazar.Calibrations.load("calibrations/default")
with blazar.Encoder(calibrations=cals, identity={"family": "wan", "version": "2.1",
                                                 "quant": "bf16", "size": "1.3b"},
                    target="balanced", backend="nvenc", codec="h264",
                    output="out.mp4") as stream:
    stream.submit(frame, width=W, height=H, fps=24.0, layout="thwc", range="unit01")
    # or, with device tensors:
    stream.submit(tensor, fps=24.0, range="unit01")

Here's a pretty simple example of using Blazar to encode frames. You can submit them one at a time or as a chunk of video, in which case they'll be mass converted to YUV and then encoded.

Peformance Comparison

This comparison table was done on a Core i7 14700KF with a 4080 Super in WSL. What we are measuring here is a BF16 (1, 3, 121, 1088, 1920) tensor being passed into the encoder pipelines for these scenarios:

  1. Blazar device bf16 (BF16 input tensor, GPU YUV conversion, NVENC)
  2. Blazar device u8 -> CPU YUV Conversion -> NVENC
  3. PyAV device u8 -> CPU YUV Conversion -> NVENC
  4. FFmpeg device u8 -> IPC -> CPU YUV Conversion -> NVENC
path ms/frame fps output vs zero-copy
blazar device bf16 (zero copy) 3.88 258 5.36 MB 1.0×
blazar host u8 6.35 158 5.34 MB 1.6×
pyav h264_nvenc (swscale) 9.37 107 3.79 MB 2.4×
ffmpeg cli h264_nvenc (pipe) 19.81 51 3.43 MB 5.1×

The optimal path is the device bf16 path. Here we feed the tensor directly into a CUDA kernel that simultaneously converts from RGB to YUV and reformats the buffer into the shape NVENC expects (T,C,H,W). On my 4080 Super we're able to hit 258 fps with 1088p tensors from SGLang. If we copy to host as a u8 that drops to 158 fps. Compared to the PyAV or FFmpeg CLI paths this is a fair improvement still.

Arm 1 thread 2 threads 4 threads scaling per-thread at 4
blazar 155.9 fps 383.0 620.8 4.0x 155.2
PyAV 33.7 61.9 63.0 1.9x 15.7

Looking at how Blazar scales with thread count you can see we 4x the throughput with 4x the threads. Really this test was to try to induce some contention in Python's GIL (Global Interpreter Lock) to test its impact on PyAV. You can see it basically caps out at 2x regardless of the number of threads.

The threads here are independent encodes, not breaking individual encodes up into threads which can improve performance at the potential cost of image quality.

Where we're at today

Today the project has support for:

  • Hardware encoders: NVENC (AV1, HEVC, AVC), VideoToolbox (HEVC, AVC)
  • Software encoders: x264, x265, vpx (VP9), svt-av1
  • Opus audio codec is currently supported
  • YUV conversion on GPU or CPU
  • fMP4 or Buffer output
  • Custom configurations

Where I want to take this

I have ideas for the future of the project. I think if we start to see some adoption there will of course be bugs and feature requests. I think that having model-aware and scene-aware encoding might be an interesting feature. I also want to explore using latents to identify regions of interest or use other signals to inform encoding decisions.

Anyway if you are running generative video models please check this project out, I am happy to take any feedback! If you want to contribute that is even better!

title: The Most Popular Open-Source Voice Cloning Model Can't Be Used Commercially
summary:
If you're building a product on open-source text-to-speech, the licence file deserves more of your attention than the demo audio. I learned this the slow way while picking models for a desktop app, and the specifics are worth writing down because the most popular option in the category is also the one you probably can't ship.

The three models worth knowing about.

Kokoro-82M — 82 million parameters, Apache 2.0, eight languages and fifty-four preset voices. It does not clone voices; you pick from its voice list. What it gives you instead is the ability to run on an ordinary CPU without a GPU anywhere in sight, which no other model here manages comfortably. For narration, app prompts, accessibility features, it's the obvious answer and the licence is the most permissive in the group.

XTTS-v2 — Coqui's model, seventeen languages, clones from a roughly six-second reference clip per its own model card. It is, by a distance, the one people search for and the one most tutorials cover. It's also the problem.

Chatterbox — Resemble AI, 500 million parameters, MIT licence, zero-shot cloning from a few seconds of audio. The base model is English only; a separate Multilingual v3 build covers twenty-three languages. Worth knowing before you ship: every output carries Resemble's PerTh watermark, which they describe as surviving MP3 compression and ordinary editing with near-perfect detection. It's inaudible and generated locally — nothing phones home — but it is detectable, and that's a product decision, not a footnote.

The licensing part.

Kokoro is Apache 2.0. Chatterbox is MIT. Both mean what you'd hope: use it, ship it, sell it, tell nobody.

XTTS-v2 is released under the Coqui Public Model License, which restricts use to non-commercial purposes. Not "attribution required", not "under a revenue threshold" — non-commercial. If you're charging for the thing you build, you're outside the licence.

Historically there was a way out: Coqui sold a commercial licence. Coqui Inc. shut down in January 2024. There is no sales team, no licensing portal, no entity to contract with. The commercial option doesn't exist at any price. So the most-downloaded, best-documented, most-searched open-source voice cloning model has no legal path into a paid product, and the reason isn't cost — it's that there's nobody left to ask.

Why this catches people.

Three things stack up. The weights are freely downloadable, which feels like permission. The ecosystem around it — community packages, wrappers, tutorials — is large and none of it leads with the licence. And "open source" does a lot of unearned work in people's heads; plenty of models described that way carry terms that aren't open source in any OSI sense.

What I'd actually do:

  1. Read the LICENSE file in the exact repository you download from, not a summary and not a blog post. Variants, community re-uploads and quantised conversions don't reliably carry the original terms.

  2. Check whether the licensor still exists. A permissive-sounding licence from a dissolved company with no successor is a different risk from the same licence backed by a live entity.

  3. Do this at model-selection time. Swapping an inference engine after you've shipped is a couple of days of work; discovering the problem after you've built a year of marketing around a model's name is a different cost entirely.

  4. Prefer Apache 2.0 or MIT when quality is close — and in this category it genuinely is close now, which wasn't true two years ago.

If you're running local TTS in anything commercial, the five minutes this takes is the cheapest five minutes in your stack.

title: Nemotron 3.5 Bolt on one GPU: what the 24 GB covers, the drafter flag and the llama.cpp trap
summary:
NVIDIA's Nemotron 3.5 Bolt 74B-A9B 24GB is a 74B agent model that reads text and images. Only about 9B of its parameters (the numbers a model learns in training) work on each token, and a token is roughly a piece of a word. Most are stored at about 2 bits each, so the file is 22.0 GB.

We served it on one A40, a 48 GB data-center card on our cloud, with llama.cpp, the open-source program most people use to run models on one machine. The image reader was on, and so was the drafter, a small helper model that speeds up writing. It used about 27 GB. For one user it wrote 136 tokens a second with the drafter and 70 without.

Three choices matter more than the model: what the 24 GB covers, which llama.cpp you compile, and when the drafter pays off. Every figure sits in our Nemotron 3.5 Bolt deployment write-up with the full measurements.

The 24 GB is a text-only budget for one user

NVIDIA's sum comes to 23.83 GB. That is 22.01 GB for the parameters, 0.87 GB of working memory for roughly 128,000 tokens of conversation, and 0.96 GB for the drafter. The image reader, another 1.68 GB, is deliberately outside the sum.

Two things eat into that margin. First, the unit: a card sold as 24 GB has 24 GiB. Read NVIDIA's figure as decimal and roughly 1.9 GB stays free; read it as GiB and only about 0.2 does. Second, the drafter took close to 2.4 GB on our A40, not 0.96. So a fit on a real 24 GB card stays unproven: we never put Bolt on one.

The recipes NVIDIA publishes for llama.cpp include the image reader, and the smallest of them asks for a 32 GB card. Our 27 GB (25.2 GiB), with the quick-start 98,304 tokens of conversation, counts the image reader too, so it does not check NVIDIA's text-only number. Measure your own server with the drafter on and off, in the unit your card is sold in.

Build the right llama.cpp, and build it in parallel

Bolt needs llama.cpp code from release day, 15 October. Kartik Gulia, an NVIDIA engineer, added the model and its image reader to llama.cpp, and ggerganov merged the change in llama.cpp pull request #30520 that same day. Older builds refuse the file.

We hit exactly that. Our worker (the agent that sets up each GPU machine for InferenceKey) pins a llama.cpp release 1,920 commits older than the merge, so we set v0.7.0 by hand.

Then compiling ate the clock. A fresh machine took 764.8 seconds from request to ready, and 705 of those went into building llama.cpp on 9 CPU cores. Our worker calls cmake --build with no parallel jobs unless CMAKE_BUILD_PARALLEL_LEVEL is set. Even with 12 jobs set by hand, the build was 92% of the wait. On a 31-core machine the same build finished in 2 minutes 41 seconds. A second copy on an already built machine was ready in 15.6 seconds. If first starts matter, count CPU cores, not only the GPU.

The drafter is a server flag, not a request option

Bolt comes with the LiLiCorr drafter, about 1.1B parameters in a 1.0 GB file. The drafter proposes several tokens ahead, Bolt verifies the whole batch in a single step, accepts the run up to its first mismatch and writes that token itself. You turn it on when the server starts:

--spec-draft-hf nvidia/NVIDIA-Nemotron-3.5-Bolt-74B-A9B-24GB-LiLiCorr-GGUF \
--spec-type draft-dflash --spec-draft-n-max 6 --spec-draft-ngl 999

On short and medium prompts it about doubled the speed: over 25 requests the median was 136 tokens a second against 70, with a floor of 110, and 70% of the drafted tokens were accepted. The per-prompt speed and acceptance table shows where it gains most.

Long documents flip the result: the drafter slows prompt reading by about a quarter. A question over a 25,000-token document took 17.5 seconds without the drafter and 21.5 seconds with it. And v0.7.0 has the per-request drafter control compiled out, so the choice is made once per server. Mixed traffic? Benchmark both shapes first.

Two traps outside the model

  • A card can report fine and still be useless. Our first two machines had RTX 5090 cards. nvidia-smi, NVIDIA's status tool, answered, but CUDA, the layer programs use to reach the GPU, failed to start. Our platform still marked the model ready, so we have no 32 GB numbers yet.
  • Hidden reasoning burns time. Bolt thinks before it replies, out of your sight. A one-sentence answer cost 374 tokens of writing time. NVIDIA's model page documents a switch to turn thinking off, and InferenceKey does not forward it yet.

What this does and does not show

The quality numbers are NVIDIA's: Bolt beats Qwen3.6-35B-A3B on most agent benchmarks (Terminal-Bench 2.1: 50.98 against 44.38) and loses on factual recall. NVIDIA's speed table puts it behind Qwen3.6 and Gemma 4. Our side was about 50 requests, one GPU, one request at a time; on a two-tool refund task it called both tools correctly in all 5 runs. We did not test several requests sharing the card, where drafters tend to help less, or vLLM, the data-center server software that is the other route.

NVIDIA built, compressed and released Bolt and its drafter under OpenMDW-1.1, which allows commercial use. Kartik Gulia and ggerganov made llama.cpp able to run it. AI Search's news video pointed us to the family. Our part was wiring it end to end and measuring it. The exact command, per-request timings and worker settings are in the complete Nemotron 3.5 Bolt article on inferencekey.com.

The 24 GB is a text-only budget for one user

NVIDIA's sum comes to 23.83 GB. That is 22.01 GB for the parameters, 0.87 GB of working memory for roughly 128,000 tokens of conversation, and 0.96 GB for the drafter. The image reader, another 1.68 GB, is deliberately outside the sum.

Two things eat into that margin. First, the unit: a card sold as 24 GB has 24 GiB. Read NVIDIA's figure as decimal and roughly 1.9 GB stays free; read it as GiB and only about 0.2 does. Second, the drafter took close to 2.4 GB on our A40, not 0.96. So a fit on a real 24 GB card stays unproven: we never put Bolt on one.

The recipes NVIDIA publishes for llama.cpp include the image reader, and the smallest of them asks for a 32 GB card. Our 27 GB (25.2 GiB), with the quick-start 98,304 tokens of conversation, counts the image reader too, so it does not check NVIDIA's text-only number. Measure your own server with the drafter on and off, in the unit your card is sold in.

Build the right llama.cpp, and build it in parallel

Bolt needs llama.cpp code from release day, 15 October. Kartik Gulia, an NVIDIA engineer, added the model and its image reader to llama.cpp, and ggerganov merged the change in llama.cpp pull request #30520 that same day. Older builds refuse the file.

We hit exactly that. Our worker (the agent that sets up each GPU machine for InferenceKey) pins a llama.cpp release 1,920 commits older than the merge, so we set v0.7.0 by hand.

Then compiling ate the clock. A fresh machine took 764.8 seconds from request to ready, and 705 of those went into building llama.cpp on 9 CPU cores. The drafter is a server flag, not a request option

Bolt comes with the LiLiCorr drafter, about 1.1B parameters in a 1.0 GB file. The drafter proposes several tokens ahead, Bolt verifies the whole batch in a single step, accepts the run up to its first mismatch and writes that token itself. You turn it on when the server starts:

The quality numbers are NVIDIA's: Bolt beats Qwen3.6-35B-A3B on most agent benchmarks (Terminal-Bench 2.1: 50.98 against 44.38) and loses on factual recall. We did not test several requests sharing the card, where drafters tend to help less, or vLLM, the data-center server software that is the other route.

NVIDIA built, compressed and released Bolt and its drafter under OpenMDW-1.1, which allows commercial use. Kartik Gulia and ggerganov made llama.cpp able to run it. AI Search's news video pointed us to the family. Our part was wiring it end to end and measuring it. The exact command, per-request timings and worker settings are in the complete Nemotron 3.5 Bolt article on inferencekey.com.

title: Jais 3: The UAE Just Built Arabic-First AI That Acts, Not Just Chats
summary:
Most AI models speak Arabic as a second language. They were built in English first, and Arabic was added later — which is why they stumble on dialects, on Egyptian or Moroccan speech, and on the everyday habit of switching between Arabic and English mid-sentence.

Jais 3, launched on 15 October 2026 by Abu Dhabi's Mohamed bin Zayed University of Artificial Intelligence (MBZUAI) and Inception42, reverses that order. It is Arabic first, and it is built to do work, not just hold a conversation.

A family, not a single model

Jais 3 is six open language models sharing one training recipe, from a 0.9-billion-parameter model designed for phones up to a 375-billion-parameter flagship for data centres. The two largest use a mixture-of-experts design — the flagship stores 375 billion parameters but activates only 23 billion per token, keeping running costs sane. Five of the six have a 512,000-token context window (the smallest has 128K), which IFM says is the longest of any Arabic-native model.

All six are on Hugging Face under the Apache 2.0 licence, so developers can use them commercially and self-host, from a phone app to a GPU cluster. They are built on K2 Horizon, IFM's open foundation model fleet from September 2026, adapted with an Arabic-focused training recipe covering Modern Standard Arabic and regional dialects, plus the cultural knowledge around the language.

The speech part is the practical win

Alongside the text models comes Jais Speech (Jais-ASR), a speech recognition system for Arabic and its dialects across 19 Arab countries. It transcribes dialects, accepts spoken instructions in Arabic or English, handles code-switching between Arabic and English or French, and applies Arabic diacritics (vowel marks) directly to live transcripts — something most speech tools skip, and which makes transcripts far more useful for documents and subtitles.

Built to act

IFM's pitch is that Jais 3 works as an agent: it plans multi-step tasks, calls tools, edits Arabic documents, searches the web and hands back a finished result. Launch examples include reading an Arabic contract, updating a spreadsheet and producing presentations. It is also designed to follow instructions closely — format, length and constraints as set by the user.

The honest caveat

Every headline benchmark number comes from IFM's own evaluations across 24 public Arabic benchmarks and has not yet been independently replicated. The most eye-catching: at 7 billion parameters, the average Arabic score rose from 56.4 for the K2 Horizon base to 79.6 after Arabic adaptation. That is a developer-reported claim, not a settled fact — and the right way to judge Jais 3 is to test it on your own dialect and documents.

Who should care

If your documents, customers and meetings are in Arabic, Jais 3 is a practical upgrade over an English-first chatbot — especially for transcription and document work. Developers building for the Arab world get six self-hostable sizes with no API bill. If you work only in English, Jais 3 still matters as a signal: language-native open models, built by countries for their own languages, are arriving fast.

This is a condensed explainer. The full breakdown — the complete model table, the benchmark picture, pros and cons, and FAQ — is on NeurAITool: Jais 3: The UAE's Open Arabic AI Family Explained.

title: A JSON state file ended in zeros after an unclean shutdown: quarantine it, then salvage every record you can
summary:
Disclosure: I'm the developer of the tool described here, and this post was drafted and published by an AI agent from the project's source code. Relaymote is unofficial; not affiliated with or endorsed by Anthropic.

Relaymote (MIT, Node.js) is a phone remote for Claude Desktop's Code-tab sessions. It keeps its task list in one file, registry.json: every queued, running and finished task, with its prompt, its dependencies and its id. It is the kind of file nobody thinks about until the day JSON.parse throws on it.

That day came after an unclean shutdown. The file had its normal size, but the last stretch of it was NUL bytes. This post is how the daemon now reacts to that: what it does at load time so it keeps running, and a separate relaymote salvage command that gets the tasks back.

What the damage looks like

The writes were already done the textbook way: write a temp file, fsync it, rename it over the real one. That protects against a half-written file from your own process. It does not fully protect you from the machine losing power around the rename, depending on the file system and what had actually reached the disk. The result we saw was a file whose length had been recorded but whose last blocks never arrived, so they read back as zeros.

The useful observation is about where the damage sits. The front of the file is intact. The break is a clean cut somewhere near the end, followed by padding. Almost every record is still there; only the parser gives up, because one bad byte fails the whole document.

Part 1: at load time, quarantine and keep going

The loader must not crash the daemon, and it must not "fix" the file in place. It does three things when parsing fails:

const q = FILE + '.corrupt-' + Date.now();
if (fs.existsSync(FILE)) {
  fs.renameSync(FILE, q);
  process.stderr.write(`registry.json could not be read; moved it to ${q}. Recover its tasks with: relaymote salvage\n`);
}
  1. Rename, never delete. The damaged file is the only copy of those tasks. Moving it aside gives the daemon a clean slate and leaves the evidence untouched.
  2. Say what to do next in the same log line. The person reading it at 2 a.m. should not have to find the docs.
  3. Keep the id counter above the damage. Task ids are t0001, t0002, and so on. If the daemon starts empty with seq = 0, new tasks will reuse ids the salvage will later bring back. So before starting empty, it scans the raw text for every id and the old seq, and starts above the highest: 
let seq = 0;
for (const m of String(raw).matchAll(/"t(\d+)"\s*:|"seq"\s*:\s*(\d+)/g))
  seq = Math.max(seq, Number(m[1] || m[2]) || 0);

A regex over broken JSON is fine here: it only needs to find numbers, not understand structure. And the new floor is saved straight away, not at the next write, so a second crash cannot lose it.

One Windows detail sits in front of all this: a file another process is renaming into place can be briefly locked (EPERM, EBUSY, EACCES). That is not corruption. The loader retries the read a few times with a short back-off before it decides the file is unreadable, so a normal save from another process never gets the registry quarantined.

Part 2: salvage, from cheapest repair to most expensive

salvage(raw) is a pure function (the tests call it directly) that tries three repairs in order and reports which one worked:

1. Trim the padding. Strip trailing NULs and whitespace, then parse. If the cut happened to land after the closing brace, this is all it takes.

2. Close the document after the last complete record. The file is written with JSON.stringify(state, null, 2), so every task object ends with a newline and exactly four spaces before its }. Find the last "\n }," (or failing that "\n }"), cut there, and append the closing braces for tasks and the root:

const cut = s.lastIndexOf('\n    },');
const j = JSON.parse(s.slice(0, cut + '\n    }'.length) + '\n  }\n}');

This leans on your own serializer's indentation, which is a fair thing to lean on: you wrote it, and it is deterministic. Everything before the last complete task comes back; only the task that was being written at the cut is lost. Any fields that came after tasks in the root object are lost too, which is why seq is recomputed from the recovered ids.

3. Scan for individual records. If the damage is in the middle, closing the document will not parse. So find each "tNNNN": {, walk forward counting braces (tracking whether you are inside a string, and escapes inside strings, so a } in a prompt doesn't end the object early), and try JSON.parse on just that slice. A mangled stretch now costs only the records it touched.

If all three fail, it returns null and the command says NOTHING_RECOVERABLE along with the file size and how much of it was padding, which is usually the whole explanation.

Part 3: merge into the live file without clobbering anything

By the time someone runs salvage, the daemon has been running on an empty registry and may have created new tasks. The recovered tasks are merged in, with a few rules:

  • Live tasks keep their ids. A recovered task whose id is taken by a different live task gets the next free id. It is renumbered, never dropped, and the renumbering is printed.
  • Dependencies follow the renumbering. If recovered task t0040 depended on t0039, and t0039 was renumbered, the dependsOn list is rewritten to match.
  • Running it twice is harmless. Each task gets a fingerprint of its creation time and prompt. A recovered task whose fingerprint already exists under any id is counted as "already present", not added again.
  • Each restored task is tagged with the corrupt file it came from, so you can tell restored tasks from new ones later.
  • Dry run by default. Without --apply it only reports: method used, characters, padding, tasks recovered, how many would be added, how many are already present, the renumbering. With --apply it writes the merged registry with the same temp-file, fsync, rename sequence. It never modifies the corrupt file, so you can run it again.

What carries over

  • When a state file fails to parse, move it aside and keep running. Never repair in place, never delete.
  • Keep id counters above anything the damaged file mentions, and persist that floor immediately.
  • Treat a briefly locked file on Windows as "retry", not "corrupt".
  • Order repairs from cheapest to most expensive and report which one worked.
  • Your own serializer's formatting is a legitimate anchor for finding record boundaries.
  • Merges should renumber rather than overwrite, follow references, and be safe to repeat.

Relaymote is MIT-licensed: github.com/ashwarsadh/relaymote. The code is in lib/registry.js and lib/salvage.js. Unofficial; not affiliated with or endorsed by Anthropic.

summary:

Ivan N founders@xerj.org
Oct 26, 2026, 12:33 PM (2 days ago)
to me

Hi Jim,

I'm Ivan, founder of XERJ, an open-source, AI-native search engine: it gives coding agents the exact passage of code or documentation they need instead of letting them guess from memory. On top of it we run a public Corpus Hub: an open index of great code solutions that agents consult before writing their own version, so they repeat what worked instead of repeating mistakes.

We reviewed your "feat(mainnet): HTML5 Ed25519 desktop node, registry mutex fix, and peer registration..." in elpresidentebutch-ctrl/synthos-collective and selected it for the hub. It is a substantial piece of work: 4 files and about 1,800 lines across cmd/cloudless-registry and cmd/silentnode, in Go.

Once it is in the hub, a developer whose coding agent hits the same kind of problem gets your implementation back as a worked reference, with your name and the repo attached, so the agent builds on code that already works instead of improvising its own version and repeating the mistakes you already solved.

If you don't mind, we will include your work in the public index, under the repo's licence (Apache-2.0) and with attribution to you and to elpresidentebutch-ctrl/synthos-collective. If you would rather keep it out, one line back is enough and I will leave it out.

And if you use AI coding agents yourself, XERJ is worth a try: it cuts the tokens an agent burns by retrieving the exact passage instead of guessing, from reference coding against real implementations to search across large document sets. It is free and open source: https://github.com/xerj-org/xerj

title: Why an Online I Ching Should Cast Six Times Before It Speaks
summary:
I have been studying the I Ching for about five years. That is long enough to know how much I still do not know—and short enough that I try not to talk like an authority.

What I do care about is the shape of the experience: how a person moves from a question, through chance, into a hexagram, and only then into words. When we started building I Ching Reflection, that order was non-negotiable. An online tool can cast in one tap. A tabletop session usually does not. We wanted the middle path: digital convenience without collapsing the ritual into a single shuffle.

This post is about that choice—why we cast six times before the reading text appears—and what we are still fixing.

The tabletop habit, in one paragraph

Classical three-coin casting is simple and slow in a good way. You hold a question. You throw three coins. Heads and tails map to a line: unbroken or broken, sometimes changing. You write that line down. You throw again. Six throws later you have a hexagram, and only then do most people open a book.

The pause between the last coin and the first sentence is not a UX bug. It is where the question settles. Online products often erase that pause because it is easy to erase: generate a random hexagram, paste an interpretation, show a share button. Fast. Also thinner.

We are not claiming that line-by-line casting is unique to us. Plenty of careful readers and apps already honor it. Our bet is narrower: if you come for an online cast, the product should still feel closer to six deliberate outcomes than to a one-tap lottery ticket.

What “lock six outcomes before any reading text” means in practice

On I Ching Reflection the flow is deliberately staged:

  1. You arrive with a question (or sit with one quietly).
  2. You cast with a three-coin model—six times, one line at a time.
  3. Each line is recorded as it lands. The hexagram is fixed by those six outcomes.
  4. Only after the hexagram is locked does reading text appear.

That fourth step is the point. The text does not steer the cast. The cast is not a decorative animation on top of a pre-chosen page. Chance first, words second.

If you have ever watched someone flip coins at a desk, you know the rhythm: throw, note, throw, note. We tried to keep that rhythm even when the “coins” are on a screen. It is slower than a single RNG call wrapped in a hexagram card. It is also closer to how many of us learned to ask.

What we are not claiming

A few lines of honesty, because the I Ching community has every right to be skeptical of shiny tools:

  • We are not selling a substitute for study. Editorial pages help you orient; they are not a replacement for sitting with a good translation and commentary over years.

title: Off Grid AI vs PocketPal (2026): The Offline Phone AI That Also Makes Images
summary:
PocketPal runs chat models on your phone. Off Grid AI Mobile (OGAM) does that too, then keeps going. It makes images, answers from your own files with sources, and syncs to an app on your computer.

Both are free and open source, and both run offline. The difference is how much your phone can do once the model is on it.

App Store · Google Play · GitHub

Free. No account. MIT licensed, with 3,300 stars on GitHub.


OGAM turns a one-line prompt into an image, on the phone. iPhone shown.

What OGAM does that PocketPal doesn't

Off Grid AI PocketPal
Make images on your phone Yes, Stable Diffusion on-device Not listed
Ask your own files, with cited answers Yes, in Projects Not listed
Speak your prompt Yes Not listed (reads replies aloud)
App for Mac, Windows and Linux Yes No, iOS and Android only
Sync chats between phone and computer Yes, with Pro No
Use a bigger model on your home computer Yes, over your own network Not listed

Checked 29 October 2026 against PocketPal's GitHub README (v1.21.4) and Off Grid AI's release notes. "Not listed" means the feature is not on PocketPal's own pages.

Your phone makes images too

Type what you want to see. OGAM writes a fuller prompt for you, then Stable Diffusion draws it on your phone. No server sees the prompt or the picture.

That matters when the image is personal, like a logo for a business you haven't announced or a picture for your kid's bedtime story. It stays in your camera roll and nowhere else.

PocketPal's README covers chat, character Pals, read-aloud voices and speed benchmarks. Image generation is not on the list. If you want words and pictures from one offline app, OGAM is the one that does both.

Ask your own files and see the source

Drop a PDF, a lease or your notes into a Project. Ask a question in plain words. OGAM answers and cites the passage it used, so you can check the claim in seconds.

The file never leaves the phone, and neither does your question. Use it on a contract before you sign, or on lecture notes the night before an exam.

Document questions are not listed in PocketPal's README.

One assistant on your phone and your computer

PocketPal lives on iOS and Android. Off Grid AI also runs on Mac, Windows and Linux as Off Grid AI Desktop (OGAD).

On a computer you get room for bigger models and a GPU for faster images. With Pro, Sync carries your chats and Projects between your devices on your own network. Start a question on the train, finish it at your desk.

Use the big model on your desk, from your phone

A phone can comfortably run a 2B to 4B model. Your computer can run far larger ones. OGAM can connect to a model server on your home network or VPN. You get the big model's answers in the phone's chat.

The traffic stays on your network. Your prompts never go to an AI company.

Which phones run it

  • iPhone 12 or newer, or Android with 4GB of RAM: small models such as Qwen 3.5 0.8B.
  • iPhone 15 Pro or a flagship Android with 8GB of RAM: Qwen 3.5 4B, the sweet spot for quality.

More RAM means larger models. The app shows which models fit before you download.

Switch in five minutes

  1. Install OGAM from the App Store or Google Play.
  2. Open the model library and download a model that fits your phone. Qwen 3.5 2B is a good first pick for 6GB to 8GB of RAM.
  3. Ask it something you'd ask in PocketPal. Then ask for an image.
  4. Make a Project, add a file and ask a question about it.

You don't need an account at any step.

What Pro adds

Pro is optional. It adds a hands-free voice mode with Kokoro, drafts you approve before anything is sent, and Sync across up to 5 devices. On 29 October 2026 it costs $79.99 once, a limited-time price down from $119, or $7.99 a month. See Pro.

The free app stays free. Chat, images, vision, voice input and Projects never need Pro.

FAQ

Does PocketPal generate images?
PocketPal's own README lists on-device chat, Pals, read-aloud and benchmarks. It does not list image generation. Off Grid AI Mobile generates images on your phone with Stable Diffusion, offline, after a one-time model download.

Can PocketPal answer questions about my documents?
Document questions are not listed in PocketPal's README. In Off Grid AI Mobile you add files to a Project and ask questions. Answers cite the passage they came from, and the files stay on your phone.

Is Off Grid AI free like PocketPal?
Yes. Chat, image generation, vision, voice input and Projects are free, with no account. Pro is optional. It adds voice mode, drafts you approve and Sync with your computer.

Can I use the same GGUF models I use in PocketPal?
Yes. Off Grid AI Mobile runs GGUF models with llama.cpp, the same format PocketPal uses. Qwen, Llama, Gemma and Phi download inside the app.

Does Off Grid AI work in airplane mode?
Yes. Once a model is downloaded, chat, image generation and Projects run on the phone with no connection.

Get it on the App Store or Google Play, download one model, and make your first image offline.

title: Off Grid AI vs Open WebUI (2026): Private ChatGPT on Your Own Device, No Server to Run
summary:
Open WebUI gives you a ChatGPT-style page for a model server you run yourself. Off Grid AI skips the server. You install one app on your computer or phone, pick a model, and the model runs inside the app. Images too.

If you want private AI without becoming a sysadmin, start here.

Download for Mac, Windows or Linux · App Store · Google Play

Free. No account. Open source on GitHub.


An image made in the chat window on the computer's own GPU. No image server to set up.

What Off Grid AI does that Open WebUI doesn't

Off Grid AI Open WebUI
Runs the model itself Yes, llama.cpp built in Connects to Ollama or an OpenAI-compatible API
What you install One app Open WebUI plus a model server
Make images with nothing else installed Yes, on your GPU or phone Through GPT-Image, Gemini or ComfyUI
iPhone and Android apps with on-device models Yes Not listed
License MIT (mobile) and AGPL-3.0 (desktop), both OSI-approved Its own Open WebUI License

Checked 29 October 2026 against docs.openwebui.com, Open WebUI's GitHub repository (v0.12.4) and Off Grid AI's release notes. "Not listed" means the feature is not on Open WebUI's own pages.

One app, no server

Open WebUI is an interface. Its docs install it with Docker, pip or a desktop app, then point it at Ollama or another OpenAI-compatible API. That's two things to install, update and keep running.

Off Grid AI Desktop (OGAD) is one download for Apple silicon Macs, Windows and Linux. The engine is inside. Pick a text model, and the app shows what fits your memory before it downloads. Then you chat. No containers, ports or second service.

Since 0.0.55, OGAD's AI engines (llama.cpp, whisper.cpp and stable-diffusion.cpp) update in the background. You get support for new models without rebuilding anything.

Images built in

Open WebUI's docs connect image generation through GPT-Image, Gemini or ComfyUI. Two of those are cloud services. The third is another server to run.

OGAD draws images on your graphics card with models such as RealVisXL V5.0 Lightning. The picture above took 6 steps at 1024 by 1024. Off Grid AI Mobile (OGAM) draws images on the phone with Stable Diffusion. Nothing leaves the device.

AI that lives on your phone

Open WebUI runs in a browser, so your phone needs a route back to your server. Away from home, that means a VPN or an open port.

OGAM runs the model on the phone. iPhone 12 and newer and Android phones with 4GB of RAM run small models. An iPhone 15 Pro runs Qwen 3.5 4B well. Chat, images, vision, voice input and Projects all work in airplane mode once a model is downloaded.

Keep your server if you like it

Already run Ollama on a big machine at home? Keep it. OGAM and OGAD can connect to a remote Ollama server on your network or VPN. You use the big model when you're home and the on-device model when you're not. One chat window either way.

Voice and documents included

OGAD listens with Whisper and answers aloud with Kokoro, on your computer. Projects answer questions about your files and cite the passage they used. Both work offline and need no add-on server.

For developers, OGAD runs one OpenAI-compatible API at 127.0.0.1:7878 that serves chat, images and speech. See the local API guide.

Switch in five minutes

  1. Download OGAD on your computer, and install OGAM from the App Store or Google Play.
  2. Download one model in each app. The apps show what fits before you download.
  3. Ask the question you last asked in Open WebUI.
  4. Ask for an image in the same chat.

No account and no server at any step.

What Pro adds

Pro is optional. It adds Sync across up to 5 devices, actions and drafts you approve, a hands-free voice mode on the phone, and searchable memory and meetings on the computer. On 29 October 2026 it costs $79.99 once, a limited-time price down from $119, or $7.99 a month. See Pro.

The free apps stay free. Chat, images, voice, Projects and the local API never need Pro.

FAQ

Does Open WebUI run AI models by itself?
Open WebUI's docs describe it as a self-hosted interface that connects to Ollama and OpenAI-compatible APIs. Off Grid AI runs the model inside the app with llama.cpp, so there is no separate server to install.

Is there a simpler alternative to Open WebUI?
Off Grid AI is one app for Mac, Windows, Linux, iPhone or Android. Install it, download a model and start chatting offline, with no Docker and no account.

Can Off Grid AI generate images like Open WebUI?
Yes, with nothing else installed. Off Grid AI generates images on your computer's GPU or on your phone. Open WebUI's docs connect image generation through GPT-Image, Gemini or ComfyUI.

Can Off Grid AI use my existing Ollama server?
Yes. Off Grid AI can connect to a remote Ollama server on your network or VPN, alongside the models it runs on the device.

Is Off Grid AI free?
Yes. The core apps are free with no account. Mobile is MIT licensed and desktop is AGPL-3.0. Pro is optional and adds memory, approved actions and Sync.

Download Off Grid AI, pick one model, and chat privately in the next five minutes.

Pick the model that fits your iPhone

MLC Chat's current version ships Llama 3.2 3B. OGAM opens a model library sized to your phone. It shows which models fit before you download.

On an iPhone 15 Pro with 8GB of RAM, Qwen 3.5 4B is the sweet spot for quality. On an iPhone 12, Qwen 3.5 0.8B runs fine. Llama, Gemma and Phi are there too, in GGUF, the format most open models ship in.

Use it for your job

MLC Chat's App Store description says it's intended for non-commercial use. That leaves client notes, contracts and other work questions in a grey area.

OGAM is MIT licensed. Use it at work, on your company's documents, with no license question hanging over it. Put a client's brief in a Project, ask what it commits you to, and draft your reply on the phone.

Your iPhone makes images

Type what you want to see. OGAM writes a fuller prompt, then Stable Diffusion draws it on the iPhone. The prompt and the picture stay on the phone.

Image generation is not listed for MLC Chat.

Your files, answered with sources

Add a PDF or your notes to a Project. Ask a question in plain words. OGAM answers and cites the passage it used, so you can check it in seconds.

The file never leaves your iPhone. Use it on a contract before you sign, or on a long report the night before a meeting.

Updated this month, and every month

OGAM shipped 8 mobile releases in October 2026. Version 0.0.118 was released on 23 October. New open models need an app that keeps up, and OGAM does.

MLC Chat's newest App Store version is from September 2024. MLC LLM, the engine behind it, is built for developers.

Your other devices

OGAM is on Google Play too. Its companion, Off Grid AI Desktop (OGAD), runs on Mac, Windows and Linux with image generation on your GPU and voice in and out.

With Pro, Sync carries your chats and Projects between iPhone and computer over your own network. Away from your desk, OGAM can reach the bigger model on your computer over your home network or VPN.

Switch in five minutes

  1. Install OGAM from the App Store.
  2. Open the model library and download a model that fits your iPhone.
  3. Ask the question you last asked in MLC Chat.
  4. Ask for an image, then add a file to a Project and ask about it.

No account at any step.

What Pro adds

Pro is optional. It adds a hands-free voice mode with Kokoro, drafts you approve before anything is sent, and Sync across up to 5 devices. On 29 October 2026 it costs $79.99 once, a limited-time price down from $119, or $7.99 a month. See Pro.

The free app stays free. Chat, images, vision, voice input and Projects never need Pro.

MLC Chat's App Store description says the app is intended for non-commercial use. Off Grid AI Mobile is MIT licensed and free to use at work.

Which models does MLC Chat include?
The current MLC Chat version on the App Store includes Llama 3.2 3B. Off Grid AI Mobile lets you choose and download GGUF models such as Qwen 3.5, Llama, Gemma and Phi, sized to your iPhone.

Does Off Grid AI run on Android too?
Yes. Off Grid AI Mobile is on Google Play as well as the App Store, and Off Grid AI Desktop runs on Mac, Windows and Linux.

Is Off Grid AI free?
Yes. The app is free with no account. Pro is optional and adds voice mode, approved drafts and Sync with your computer.
